📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FY 2027 Transportation Proposal Puts EV Charging Investments at Risk.

Sources indicate that WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Monday, Senate Republicans released an Appropriations package that proposes to take back nearly $2 billion in federal funding already allocated to states to build out electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and repurpose it for general transportation uses, putting critical clean transportation investments at risk.

Republicans already clawed back roughly $500 million from the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program in the FY 2026 appropriations bill. Now, they are proposing to further divert these funds, even as all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico have approved aims for their use and are working to deliver critical charging infrastructure to their communities. More than half of available NEVI funding has already been committed to projects, and the proposal threatens to upend additional awards that states continue to make to charging developers.

According to recent reports, for example, Texas recently made an announcement of $226 million in awards that will support 321 stations. The Senate proposal would threaten Texas’s remaining NEVI funding, along with funding for states like Ohio, which has one of the largest numbers of operational NEVI-funded stations in the country.

In response, Clean Transportation for All Director Katherine García released the following statement:.

“It is unacceptable for Senate Republicans to once again seek to claw back critical EV charging investments. Trump’s day-one freeze of NEVI set states back, and they are only now back on track after we successfully challenged that freeze in court. This latest proposal threatens affordable transportation for American families, clean air for communities, and states’ efforts to build the infrastructure of the future. We have successfully defended NEVI against the Trump administration’s attacks, and we will continue fighting to protect the program and ensure these investments reach communities across the country.”.

The NEVI program, established through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021, provides funding to states to build a nationwide network of EV fast-charging stations. Protecting that investment is essential to expanding charging access, supporting EV adoption, reducing dependence on volatile gasoline prices, and cutting transportation pollution.

Since the Trump administration’s unlawful freeze of the NEVI program was lifted following successful litigation by Sierra Club, its partners, and a coalition of states, hundreds of millions of dollars in NEVI funding have been committed to charging projects.

Congress must preserve funding for EV charging infrastructure while providing dedicated resources for passenger rail, public transit, and other clean transportation priorities.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott discusses H-1B visas and immigration to his state on 'The Will Cain Show.'.

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) said she intends to rescind Gov. Greg Abbott’s hiring freeze on H-1B visa workers at state agencies and public universities on her first day in office, even as she acknowledged that the federal visa program has been abused.

In a recent interview with the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa, a Democrat, dismissed Abbott’s January directive restricting fresh H-1B visa petitions as a distraction.

"Yeah, that does not make sense to me. I will tell you, I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do," Hinojosa said.

Abbott issued the order in January to bar state agencies and public universities from filing newly introduced H-1B petitions without written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission, citing reports that employers had displaced U. S. workers with lower-paid foreign labor.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP’S BID TO PROTECT US JOBS BY REFORMING CONTROVERSIAL IMMIGRATION POLICY.

Industry observers note that governor-elect Gina Hinojosa speaks at a press conference Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at The University of Texas at Austin. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images).

"In the most egregious schemes, employers have even fired American workers and replaced them with H-1B employees, often at lower wages," Abbott wrote in his January directive.

While Hinojosa vowed to scrap the restrictions, she conceded that companies have exploited the visa system.

In a recent development, "There are abuses when it comes to H-1Bs, absolutely," Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune. "Companies should not be getting a bunch of tax breaks for jobs to only then use that money to hire H-1B employees. That’s wrong. That’s happening right now. I don’t support that.".

It has been revealed that hinojosa, a Democratic state representative from Austin, defeated Abbott in the Nov. 3 election to deny the three-term Republican incumbent a fourth term, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990. With Republicans still holding a majority in the Texas Senate, rescinding Abbott’s executive orders offers Hinojosa an immediate way to reshape state policy without legislative approval.

HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT FUELS 11TH-HOUR POWER STRUGGLE AS LATEST ALLIES RALLY TO REIN IN INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR.

According to recent reports, texas Gov. Greg Abbott immediately halted newly introduced H-1B visas. (Getty Images).

Hinojosa also defended local school districts’ use of H-1B visas to recruit foreign educators, arguing that Texas schools struggle to find domestic teachers. Abbott’s directive, however, applies only to state agencies and public institutions of higher education, not local K-12 school districts.

  • energy storage industry installed 14.3 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of new capacity in Q3, bringing total installations in the first nine months of 2026 to 48.3 GWh, according to the U.S.
  • energy storage capacity installed has now exceeded 200 GWh to date as grid operators, utilities, and energy buyers turn to storage to lower energy costs and strengthen grid reliability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rapid Growth in Energy Storage Is Helping Stabilize Electricity Prices and Strengthen Grid Reliability; Industry Urges Congress to Pass Permitting Reform to Accelerate Deployment.

LAS VEGAS — The U.S. energy storage industry installed 14.3 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of new capacity in Q3, bringing total installations in the first nine months of 2026 to 48.3 GWh, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO) released today by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

It has been revealed that U.S. energy storage capacity installed has now exceeded 200 GWh to date as grid operators, utilities, and energy buyers turn to storage to lower energy costs and strengthen grid reliability. After voters sent a clear message in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs must be a priority, the U.S. solar and storage industry is urging lawmakers to send the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) to the President’s desk.

Last week, more than 300 solar and storage companies sent a letter to Congressional leadership urging swift passage of BAAJA. The legislation will accelerate energy storage deployment, reduce project costs, and expand access to lower-cost, reliable electricity for households and businesses.

“Voters made it clear that they want lower prices, and the growing deployment of energy storage is helping make that happen. We’re urging Congress to pass BAAJA to build out America’s energy infrastructure and put downward pressure on prices,” noted SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty.

Recent findings suggest that the outlook for energy storage continues to strengthen, with the report increasing its 2030 cumulative U.S. deployment forecast by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid and BTM. The revised forecast reflects sustained industry momentum, with U.S. installations up 20% year over year through the first nine months of 2026.

Texas led the nation in utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona and California followed with 7.7 GWh and 6.8 GWh, respectively. Recent SEIA analysis highlights that rapid growth in solar and energy storage helped drive down average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California from summer 2021 to summer 2026.

11 states surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records in Q3, even with three months remaining in 2026: Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, Senior Analyst at Benchmark Minerals. “Across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, energy storage pipelines are growing as a result of both investment appetite and flexibility requirements.”.

According to recent reports, U.S. storage manufacturing continues to accelerate, ensuring that more of the batteries being deployed to strengthen the grid are made in the United States. In July, a new battery cell manufacturing facility opened in Tennessee. In October, a new cell manufacturing facility opened in Indiana, bringing total cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% increase.

Utility-scale projects accounted for the vast majority of Q3 installations, with 12.2 GWh deployed, followed by 1.3 GWh of commercial and industrial storage, and 746 MWh of residential storage.

This month, Nextnova celebrated the official inauguration of its new solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City, marking an notable milestone in strengthening America’s domestic solar manufacturing industry.

The facility will manufacture high-efficiency solar cells using advanced automation, Industry 4.0 technologies, and comprehensive digital traceability.

Production is scheduled to begin in March 2027 with an initial annual capacity of 2 GW, designed to expand to 5 GW as market demand grows.

The new factory is expected to create approximately 300 skilled jobs in engineering, manufacturing, quality assurance, and operations, supporting economic growth while reinforcing the U.S. clean energy supply chain.

Nextnova celebrates the inauguration of its new solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City. Credit: Nextnova.

In a recent development, “Today represents an exciting milestone for Nextnova and for American solar manufacturing,” said Nathan Kii Miller, Nextnova’s chief strategy officer, in a statement. “Our Oklahoma City facility combines advanced manufacturing technology, complete supply chain transparency, and rigorous quality standards to deliver premium solar cells while strengthening a resilient domestic solar industry.”.

Designed for maximum quality and reliability, the facility features fully integrated manufacturing execution systems (MES), automated inspection technologies, advanced process control, and a dedicated analytical laboratory supporting continuous quality verification throughout production.

Recent findings suggest that nextnova notes that its commitment to transparent sourcing, manufacturing excellence, and scalable production provides customers with high-performance solar cells that support the continued growth of a secure and competitive U.S. solar industry.

Third Pillar Constructing Largest Floating Solar Complex in New York

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that crown City Solar will be North America’s first floating community solar project.
  • — Third Pillar Power today confirmed it is constructing Crown City Solar, North America’s first floating community solar project, at Suit-Kote Corporation’s Polkville Crushed Stone Facility, an active sand and gravel mining operation co-located with an asphalt plant and storage terminal in Cortlandville, N.Y.
  • Crown City Solar 1 is the first of three 7.5 MW-dc phases and is expected to begin commercial operation in February 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that crown City Solar will be North America’s first floating community solar project. Phases 1 and 2 are under construction, and the three-phase, 22.5 MW DC complex is expected to be fully operational in 2027.

CORTLANDVILLE, N.Y. — Third Pillar Power today confirmed it is constructing Crown City Solar, North America’s first floating community solar project, at Suit-Kote Corporation’s Polkville Crushed Stone Facility, an active sand and gravel mining operation co-located with an asphalt plant and storage terminal in Cortlandville, N.Y.

Crown City Solar 1 is the first of three 7.5 MW-dc phases and is expected to begin commercial operation in February 2027. Crown City Solar 2 and Crown City Solar 3 are scheduled to begin commercial operation in October 2027, bringing the site to 22.5 MW-dc in total and making Crown City Solar North America’s largest floating solar complex. The complex takes its name from nearby Cortland, known locally as the Crown City because it sits on an elevated plain over 1,000 feet above sea level.

“Every quarry and reservoir in this country already has a job to do. Crown City Solar shows that those sites can take on a second one: powering their neighbors through a Central Fresh York winter, at a community scale, on a working industrial site. The question is no longer whether floating solar works here. It’s how quickly we can bring it to the next site, like Polkville, and the one after that,” said Jaimeet Gulati, CEO of Third Pillar Power.

Recent findings suggest that third Pillar identified the approximately 120-acre flooded mine pit as an ideal host for the project in early 2024. Thanks to the collaborative efforts of Suit-Kote, the Town of Cortlandville, and Cortland County, the project team brought this first-of-its-kind project to construction less than two years after securing site control and applying for interconnection. Suit-Kote was acquired by Colas USA, the U.S. subsidiary of Colas, in October 2026.

Recent findings suggest that crown City Solar also represents a series of technical firsts. It is engineered for the conditions of a Central New York winter, including a ground snow load of 69 pounds per square foot, the highest of any floating solar project in the country. Additionally, the project will float its medium-voltage transformers and switchgear on custom-designed barges—another first for a U.S. floating solar project. Floating this equipment further reduces the use of agricultural land, addresses floodplain siting concerns, and improves electrical efficiency. These firsts reflect Third Pillar’s specialization in floating solar, from identifying and engineering projects on working industrial water bodies to securing the permits and interconnection needed to bring them online.

According to recent reports, D3Energy is serving as the engineering, procurement, and construction contractor. The floating system uses Alps’ Solar PV modules, Hazelett Marine’s specialized elastic mooring systems, and Profloating’s floats.

Sources indicate that “With more than a decade of building floating solar projects across the country, D3Energy is proud to bring that experience to a project of this magnitude. Crown City Solar demonstrates what is possible with floating solar. We’re grateful for our partnership with Third Pillar Power and the trust they’ve placed in D3Energy to help bring North America’s largest floating solar complex to life,” noted Stetson Tchividjian, Managing Director of D3Energy.

Crown City Solar 1 is expected to achieve mechanical completion in December 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it is known.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has issued a latest briefing published to coincide with the UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye.
  • Plastic already emits more than two billion tons of CO₂e a year, about twice as much as aviation, and under current policies this would more than double as the fossil fuel industry turns to plastic as its hedge against electrification.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it is known. Plastic is a major cause of the climate crisis, yet governments continue to ignore it.

Recent findings suggest that the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has issued a latest briefing published to coincide with the UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye. The briefing, “Reducing plastic production in a post-1.5°C world: A test of resolve for the international community,” calls on governments to reduce global plastic production.

Plastic already emits more than two billion tons of CO₂e a year, about twice as much as aviation, and under current policies this would more than double as the fossil fuel industry turns to plastic as its hedge against electrification.

“There’s only so much carbon the world can still emit if we want to avoid blasting past the Paris Agreement targets. Plastic’s harm to our climate is happening in plain sight, and governments are choosing to look away. Every latest plastics plant locks in decades of emissions the planet simply cannot afford. As leaders gather at COP31, they must recognise plastic as a major cause of carbon pollution that is rapidly heating our world.” — Steve Trent, CEO, Environmental Justice Foundation.

Over 90% of plastic emissions come before a plastic product is even used, during extraction, conversion and production. If current policies remain unchanged, global plastic production is projected to almost triple by 2060, and annual emissions from fossil-based plastics to more than double, to 4.3 billion tons of CO2e.

Recent findings suggest that on this trajectory, plastics would emit 67 billion tons of CO2e between 2026 and 2050. That is just over half of the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of meeting the 1.5°C target, and 27% of the budget for a very good chance of limiting the overshoot to 1.7°C. None of this is hidden; emissions are quantified, the projections are published and the industry’s expansion intends are public, yet plastic remains on the margins of climate negotiations.

EJF is calling on governments at COP31 to recognize plastic for what it is: a major driver of climate change that must be tackled at its source, by cutting production.

The petrochemical industry’s bet on plastics.

As the world electrifies transport and power, the fossil fuel industry is using plastic as its hedge against electrification. With oil demand for transport and energy expected to decline, petrochemical companies are pivoting to plastics to keep oil and gas flowing. The plastics sector could account for 20% of global oil consumption by 2050, up from around 12% today. The top fifteen petrochemical companies received an estimated US$590.8 billion in financing between 2019 and 2025, and the sector was propped up by state subsidies estimated at over $80 billion in 2024 alone, almost half of which came from Saudi Arabia.

A test of resolve for the plastics treaty.

In a recent development, A total of 145 countries from every continent have expressed support for provisions to reduce plastic production during the global plastics treaty negotiations. Rwanda and Peru have proposed a global target to cut plastic production by 40% by 2040 against a 2025 baseline. Modelling cited in the briefing demonstrates that a 40% cut in high-ambition countries, joined by China and emerging producers, could reduce global emissions from plastics by as much as 21% compared with business as usual.

Industry observers note that but negotiations have reached a deadlock, driven by a small group of oil- and plastic-producing states, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran and China, with the United States recently aligning with their position. At least 234 fossil fuel and chemical industry lobbyists attended the latest round of talks in Geneva — more than the combined delegations of the EU and its 27 Member States.

At COP31, EJF is urging governments to:.

Final Thoughts about Plastic and our Leaders.

The truth about plastics is perverse. Plastics are widely used around the world due to ease of manufacturing, low cost, stable chemical properties, and good water resistance. They have infiltrated every part of the environment and human life cycle. More than 16,000 chemicals are used in manufacturing plastics, and at least 4,200 of these have been identified as hazardous to human health and the environment. Thousands more chemicals used in plastic production have never been tested. Many of these chemicals migrate out of plastic packaging into our foods, drinks, household products, and bodies.

It has been revealed that researchers have come up with many possible solutions to plastic pollution, as well as ways to mitigate microplastics in the environment. But will governments have the wherewithal to stand up to the powerful fossil fuel lobby that is behind plastic propaganda?

#53787. Industry News: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1708 w)

Industry News: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Npr

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, federal judges have issued temporary restraining orders to block construction of Trump's arch and keep East Potomac Park open.
  • A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C.
  • District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, federal judges have issued temporary restraining orders to block construction of Trump's arch and keep East Potomac Park open. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption.

A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.

D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.

Recent findings suggest that chutkan's newly introduced five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.

"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.

The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.

That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

According to recent reports, "This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.

Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Industry observers note that critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.

A jogger passes a mobile security camera truck at Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build his arch. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption.

The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

It has been revealed that in court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump remarked in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the looks that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "right now in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch.".

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.".

The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.

Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.

Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.

Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.

Industry observers note that but the golf course itself is at the moment unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.

Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is presently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.

Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal concerns and decides whether to concern a longer preliminary injunction.

It has been revealed that the government, on the other hand, noted "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.

In a recent development, national Park Service employees walk past a golfer at East Potomac Park on Monday, after a judge ordered the administration to keep the park open. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption.

In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its proposal for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.

Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.

The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department stated deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).

Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any blueprint that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.

In a recent development, commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.

Recent findings suggest that vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, mentioned there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.

According to recent reports, cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has remarked it prepares to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.

Administration officials stated in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.

It has been revealed that plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.

"In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.

Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political.".

Recent findings suggest that "Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of promptly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!".

According to recent reports, government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its aims for the park.

Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Social leasing could soon change in scale, name, and business model. The bill introduced by MP Christine Arrighi aims to create a public service offering one million “low-cost electric vehicles” (ALM). Scheduled for December 3rd in the National Assembly, its examination is expected to place at the heart of the debate a now crucial question: how to make social leasing sustainable and widespread?

In a recent development, several presidential candidates have made reaching one million vehicles (or even more) one of the hallmarks of their campaigns¹. While this convergence is excellent news, the battle of figures claims nothing about how to achieve this goal.

The current system cannot simply be scaled up twentyfold. Its cost per vehicle, intermittent financing, imperfect social targeting, lack of a guaranteed solution after three years, and the resale risks borne by dealerships are all structural limitations. The 2026 edition also revealed its dependence on Renault and Stellantis, which can at any time restrict volumes to favor more profitable traditional sales.

The proposed law changes its approach. Sponsored by MP Christine Arrighi, it draws inspiration from the proposals of T&E France and Bernard Julien, stemming from their study on the future of social leasing, published in June 2026.

Industry observers note that in this new model, the government would directly purchase the vehicles at an average net cost of €15,000. These vehicles would be kept for twelve years in a public fleet and leased successively to one or more households for an average monthly rent of €150 before being resold. The day-to-day management of the fleet would be delegated to groups of public or private operators within the local areas.

The initial investment to build the fleet would be financed by borrowing, with a maximum outstanding amount of €7.8 billion in 2035. Lease payments and resales, supplemented by €350 million in annual public support (equivalent to the current social leasing budget), would cover service costs and repay the debt within eighteen years. By then, the system would be self-financing, and the state would own one million cars worth approximately €10 billion.

“This model is much more beneficial for public finances,” explains Diane Strauss, director of T&E France. “It requires an initial funding effort, but it eventually pays for itself. Instead of subsidizing at a loss, we build up an asset that generates its own revenue. This is what makes the move to a million vehicles financially viable.”.

According to recent reports, in addition to providing long-term protection for low-income motorists against rising and volatile fuel prices, the proposal represents a genuine industrial planning policy. The announcement of a public order for two million vehicles over twenty years (including fleet renewal) would indeed give the French automotive sector the visibility necessary to invest and prepare for the future.

“This will also allow us to direct our production towards the vehicles that households truly need: affordable, fuel-efficient, repairable electric cars, produced in France and Europe,” concludes Léo Larivière, automotive transition expert at T&E France. “This proposal must now open a substantive discussion among all stakeholders. It is high time to prepare the next steps for one of the rare examples of policies that reconcile climate, social justice, and industrial planning.”.

Sources indicate that ¹ Raphaël Glucksmann and Marine Tondelier aim for one million vehicles. Jean-Luc Mélenchon proposes a public fleet of 1.4 million cars by 2032, and François Ruffin raises the target to three million. Gabriel Attal and Dominique de Villepin also advocate expanding social leasing, without specifying a target.
